newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia faces coffee rise on market surge.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia faces coffee rise on market surge.

text.p: Australia's coffee prices are likely to rise soon if the world market continues to ride high, a spokesman for the Australian Tea and Coffee Traders Association said on Thursday.
All roasters will be looking at their individual situation with the focus on stocks held, the spokesman said.
"If it (price crunch-time) hasn't come already it's pretty soon," he said. "Everyone's waiting for somebody to make the first move."

Australian coffee roasters and retailers have hung on for months without increasing prices, partly insulated from surging world market prices by buffer stocks of six to eight weeks and restrained by local competitive pressure.
But stocks of coffee purchased at lower prices are nearing exhaustion, although major players in the industry declined to discuss their individual positions.
Last month the Australian Tea and Coffee Association told Reuters that Australian coffee roasters would look at a price rise in April if world prices did not fall significantly.
Since then, world prices have continued to boom, with New York prices up 17 percent in the past four days to their highest level in more than two years.
Peter Kelly, general manager corporate services of Swiss-owned Nestle Australia Ltd, declined comment on whether Nestle might raise its prices soon and on Nestle's inventory situation.

Nestle holds 70 percent of Australia's instant coffee market and has 54 percent of the country's total coffee market, by volume. The company's overall share of the Australian coffee market by value is 45 percent.
Nestle had not raised coffee prices in Australia, he said.
The Tea and Coffee Association spokesman, who asked that he not be named, said that none of the significant players in the Australian market had raised their prices in recent times.
This partly reflected local competition after a price cut by Nestle in January.

Possible price rises depended on the inventories of individual companies but there was no defined time relationship between inventories and price rises, Nestle's Kelly said on Thursday in response to questions about when prices might rise.
Leading upmarket department store retailer David Jones Ltd, which negotiates its coffee prices with suppliers bi-annually, had not increased prices, a buyer said.
But the company was entering into negotiations in three weeks time. It was hoped that prices could be maintained for as long as possible, she said.
The Tea and Coffee Association representative said there were no signs of the world market price rise abating.
